paper_title: Think Less, Locally: Local Preference Learning for Reasoning Compression

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large reasoning models achieve strong performance on challenging tasks, but their long chain-of-thought often incurs substantial inference costs by continuing to deliberate after sufficient information has been obtained. Existing reasoning compression methods primarily operate on reasoning trajectories, paying less attention to the local decision of whether further reasoning is necessary given the current state. We propose LoCo, a local preference learning method for reasoning compression. LoCo detects candidate overthinking states from the model's own traces, freezes the corresponding reasoning prefixes, regenerates shorter verified continuations from the same states, and trains on the resulting state-conditioned preference pairs with DPO. This formulation teaches the model when to continue reasoning and when to conclude, rather than simply encouraging shorter trajectories overall. We construct training data entirely from self-generated mathematical traces and evaluate LoCo on five mathematical and three code generation benchmarks. LoCo reduces completion length by 41.7\%--45.4\% on mathematics and 23.4\%--36.3\% on code, while maintaining or improving accuracy and achieving the best AUC across all code benchmarks. LoCo consistently improves the accuracy-efficiency trade-off on mathematics and transfers effectively to code generation despite math-only training, demonstrating the cross-domain generality of local preference learning for reasoning compression. The code and model will be publicly released at https://github.com/MuyaoYuan/LoCo.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Large reasoning models (LRMs) (Guo et al., 2025) have made remarkable progress on complex reasoning tasks such as mathematical problem solving and algorithmic programming. This progress is largely driven by extended chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, in which models generate thousands of tokens for hypothesis formation, calculation, revision, and verification before arriving at an answer (Muennighoff et al., 2025). Such extended reasoning comes at substantial inference cost, significantly increasing decoding latency and memory consumption during deployment. More importantly, longer reasoning does not necessarily lead to higher accuracy, as models may continue reasoning beyond what is necessary to reach correct answer (Chen et al., 2024; Sui et al., 2025). This tendency to engage in excessive reasoning is commonly referred to as overthinking. Recent studies indicate that when the task is solvable by the model, overthinking is more closely related to model preference than reasoning capability (Zhang et al., 2026a; Peng et al., 2025). model may get the correct answer early in the reasoning process yet continue generating unnecessary reasoning, reflecting preference to keep thinking rather than to stop when sufficient reasoning has been reached. The problem therefore lies in when the model chooses to stop, rather than whether it can reach the correct answer (Chen et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2026a). Mitigating overthinking thus Equal contribution. Work done at WeChat AI. Corresponding authors: < zhangwzh@xjtu.edu.cn, withtomzhou@tencent.com> Project lead: Liyan Xu <liyanlxu@tencent.com>

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: calls for aligning models toward concise reasoning behaviors, which can be learned from carefully curated self-generated reasoning traces (Shen et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026b). Toward this objective, existing self-generated methods derive compression supervision in two main ways, through trajectory-level signals and fine-grained operations within the reasoning process. Trajectory-level signals are derived from the reasoning trajectory as whole, using global properties of complete solutions to establish preference for more concise reasoning. Specifically, one line of work (Team et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2026; Shen et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2025) constructs preference pairs by comparing shorter and longer correct solutions, encouraging the model to favor the shorter one, while another (Arora & Zanette, 2026; Aggarwal & Welleck, 2025; Hu et al., 2026) incorporates length preferences into reinforcement learning by rewarding shorter correct reasoning. Fine-grained operations provide more localized alternative by modifying parts of an existing reasoning trajectory. Specifically, these methods remove redundant content (Xia et al., 2025), compress individual reasoning steps (Jang et al., 2024), or shorten continuations from intermediate reasoning states to construct training data for more concise reasoning (Lai et al., 2024; Jin et al., 2025). Such operations are well aligned with recent findings (Xu et al., 2026) that LLM reasoning proceeds through local and incremental state transitions rather than globally planned process. However, existing fine-grained methods still treat the reasoning trajectory itself as the object of compression. They focus on which parts of the trajectory should be removed or shortened, rather than whether further reasoning is necessary given the models current state. This distinction is crucial because the appropriate compression decision can vary across reasoning states: the model may need to continue reasoning at one state but should conclude at another. Building on this observation, we propose LoCo (Local Compression), local preference learning method for reasoning compression. LoCo identifies overthinking states from the models own reasoning process and constructs state-conditioned preferences by contrasting alternative continuations from the same reasoning state. The resulting supervision is grounded in the models own reasoning trajectories and actual reasoning behavior. By making the compression decision conditional on the current reasoning state, LoCo encourages the model to conclude when further reasoning is unnecessary while preserving its ability to continue reasoning when additional computation is needed. In this way, LoCo avoids indiscriminate compression across the reasoning trajectory and reduces the risk of compromising the models reasoning capability on more challenging problems. We construct training data from self-generated traces and evaluate LoCo on five mathematical reasoning benchmarks and three coding benchmarks spanning broad range of difficulty. The experiments show that LoCo consistently achieves the strongest efficiencyperformance trade-off on mathematics, with especially clear advantages on the harder datasets where both high compression and high accuracy are required. The same trained model also transfers effectively to coding benchmarks of different difficulty, supporting the view that LoCo improves chain-of-thought compression by reshaping the models reasoning preference rather than by injecting additional task-specific knowledge. To summarize, our main contributions are threefold: We show that effective reasoning compression requires state-aware decisions about when further reasoning is unnecessary, rather than simply favoring shorter trajectories. We introduce LoCo, local preference learning framework that identifies overthinking states and learns continue-or-conclude preferences from verified continuations sharing the same reasoning prefix. We demonstrate the effectiveness of LoCo across mathematical reasoning and code generation, with consistent improvements in the efficiency-performance trade-off and strong cross-domain generalization.

sections.title: 2.1 TRAJECTORY-LEVEL COMPRESSION
sections.content: Several reasoning compression methods formulate compression supervision at the trajectory level, treating complete reasoning traces as the unit of comparison. Kimi k1.5 (Team et al., 2025) introduces Long2Short stage that contrasts correct short and long solutions generated by the model

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: itself and optimizes their relative preference with DPO. O1-Pruner (Luo et al., 2026) follows similar paradigm by applying preference fine-tuning to pre-sampled responses, encouraging the model to favor more concise reasoning. CoT-Valve (Ma et al., 2025) identifies parameter-space direction for controlling reasoning length, then learns from globally shortened reasoning traces. Another group of methods (Arora & Zanette, 2026; Aggarwal & Welleck, 2025; Hu et al., 2026) incorporates reasoning length into the reinforcement learning objective, jointly rewarding solution quality and efficient token usage under prescribed length budget. Collectively, these studies show that reasoning can often be shortened without substantially affecting problem-solving performance. However, these methods generally compare or optimize complete reasoning trajectories, which provides an overall preference for shorter solutions but offers less information about where the unnecessary reasoning occurs. Two solutions may reach the same answer through different reasoning paths, making it difficult to determine which part of the reasoning can be safely shortened from their overall length or preference alone. This motivates more fine-grained approach that identifies unnecessary deliberation at specific points in the reasoning process.

sections.title: 2.2 FINE-GRAINED COMPRESSION
sections.content: Fine-grained operations offer more localized way to reduce reasoning by modifying selected parts of an existing trajectory. These methods remove redundant content, compress individual reasoning steps, or shorten continuations from intermediate states, in line with recent findings that LLM reasoning proceeds through local and incremental state transitions rather than globally planned process (Xu et al., 2026). One line of work removes redundant content from the trajectory itself. TokenSkip (Xia et al., 2025) prunes verbose tokens, Verbosity-Aware Rationale Reduction (Jang et al., 2024) removes redundant sentences based on principled likelihood criteria, and Reasoning Shaping (Song et al., 2025) reweights computation-heavy segments during RLVR training. TokenSqueeze (Zhang et al., 2026b) combines depth-matched data selection with distribution-aligned token-level linguistic refinement and achieves strong performance on standard benchmarks. Another line operates at the step level. Step-DPO (Lai et al., 2024) introduces preference pairs of correct and erroneous continuations sharing the same prefix, while SSPO (Xu et al., 2025) and ReCUT (Jin et al., 2025) adapt this formulation to reasoning compression and encourage more concise step-level reasoning. Despite their finer granularity, these approaches mainly derive compression signals by contrasting or modifying existing reasoning content. Such supervision is effective for identifying unnecessary tokens, sentences, or steps, but provides less direct guidance on the decision to continue reasoning from particular state. LoCo addresses this aspect by anchoring the comparison at fixed reasoning state and learning preferences over its alternative continuations. This formulation captures the local decision of whether further deliberation is warranted while retaining the original state as shared context.

sections.title: 3 PRELIMINARIES
sections.content: Large Reasoning Models and Reasoning States. Large reasoning models (LRMs), such as DeepSeek-R1 (Guo et al., 2025), are trained to perform extended reasoning before producing final answer. Given problem q, model first generates chain of thought (CoT) = (s0, s1, . . . , sn), consisting of intermediate hypotheses, calculations, revisions, and verifications, before arriving at the final answer. The reasoning process is typically enclosed by dedicated thinking tags, such as <think> and </think> in DeepSeek-R1 (Guo et al., 2025), with paragraph breaks naturally separating different reasoning moves. We therefore segment the CoT into reasoning steps at paragraph boundaries and denote each step by si. reasoning step may correspond to establishing subgoal, performing computation, verifying an intermediate result, or drawing conclusion. We denote the input prompt associated with question as prompt(q), which includes the task instruction and the question itself. For notational convenience, we define the reasoning state after step si as Pi = prompt(q) s0 si, (1) where denotes concatenation. Thus, Pi contains all information available after completing si and before generating si+1. Each state therefore defines local decision point at which the model can either continue reasoning or conclude. We view overthinking as continuing to generate additional

Low confidence can arise from genuinely difficult sub-problem, while high volatility can accompany legitimate change in reasoning. Their combination instead identifies states where the model is both uncertain and unstable. The detector is causal by construction: both ci and vi are computed from information available by the end of step si, whereas truncation begins only from si+1. Hence, the detector never uses the continuation it removes. Judge Re-checking. Confidence alone cannot reliably distinguish redundant deliberation from genuine difficulty. We therefore re-examine each flagged state with stronger judge model J. The two stages use different evidence. The screen identifies candidates solely from the confidence statistics (ci, vi), while the judge reads the current reasoning state and determines whether the next step is redundant. The next step is classified as OVERTHINK if it re-deliberates on information that has already been established, NORMAL if it makes substantive progress, or FINAL if it presents the answer. This distinction matters because truncation from Pi should remove only redundant continuation. Removing NORMAL step discards useful progress, while removing FINAL step may discard the answer itself. This case is particularly relevant because reasoning models often conclude their CoT by restating or boxing the final answer, which may appear repetitive but is necessary for answer extraction. sections.title: 5.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: Data Construction and Training Configurations. The preference data are constructed from selfgenerated traces of DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B on the math-only training set used by Zhang et al. (2026b). For each query, we sample three rollouts with temperature 0.6 and top-p 0.95, and use the shortest correct rollout as the original trajectory. We then re-examine each flagged reasoning step with Qwen3-30B as the judge. For each detected step, we regenerate = 8 continuations using the same temperature and top-p, and retain preference pairs with at least δ = 300 tokens of savings, while limiting each question to at most = 3 pairs. The prompt and continuation lengths are capped at cp = 6k and cr = 12k tokens, respectively. We train DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B with LoCo for two epochs using LoRA adapter. The adapter has rank 256, scaling factor α = 512, and dropout 0.05 on the q/k/v/o attention projections, while the base model remains frozen. We use an effective batch size of 64 and learning rate of 1 105, with cosine schedule and warmup ratio of 0.1. Optimization uses AdamW with weight decay of 0.01 and gradient clipping of 1.0. The DPO temperature is set to β = 0.1, with the base model serving as the reference policy. Training is conducted on four H20 GPUs with maximum sequence length of 14,336 tokens. Evaluation. We evaluate LoCo on mathematical reasoning and code generation. For mathematical reasoning, we use five benchmarks spanning different difficulty levels: MATH-500 (Lightman et al., 2024) with 500 problems, AMC 2023 with 40 problems, Olympiad (He et al., 2024) with 675 problems, AIME 2024 with 30 problems, and AIME 2025 with 30 problems. For code generation, we use MBPP (Austin et al., 2021) sanitized with 257 problems, LiveCodeBench (Jain et al., 2025) release v5 with 167 problems, and CodeContests (Li et al., 2022) with 165 problems. We sample eight completions per problem for all benchmarks. Evaluation is performed with vLLM using the LoRA adapter and batched generation, with temperature 0.6 and top-p 0.95. We allow up to 32,768 newly generated tokens with context length of 36,864, and generate until EOS without truncating at </think>. sections.title: 5.2 EVALUATION ON MATHEMATICAL REASONING BENCHMARKS
sections.content: We first evaluate LoCo on mathematical reasoning benchmarks that span wide difficulty range, from MATH-500 and AMC23 to Olympiad, AIME24, and AIME25. This setting tests whether the method can compress reasoning aggressively without sacrificing performance as problem difficulty increases. Table 1 shows consistent pattern across difficulty levels. On the easier benchmarks, LoCo already matches or improves upon the base model while removing 41.7%44.1% of the generated tokens. More importantly, this advantage becomes even clearer on the harder benchmarks: on Olympiad, AIME24, and AIME25, LoCo simultaneously attains the highest accuracy, the highest AUC, and 44.6%45.4% reduction in completion length. This behavior distinguishes LoCo from both baselines. DAST provides only mild compression and can even increase completion length on harder benchmarks, while TokenSqueeze compresses aggressively but loses more accuracy as difficulty rises. Overall, the results indicate that LoCo preserves reasoning quality under substantial compression and remains particularly strong exactly where preserving difficult reasoning matters most.

Compared with this external-continuation variant, LoCo performs better overall in compression and AUC, especially on the harder AIME benchmarks. plausible explanation is distributional alignment. The preference pairs in LoCo are built from continuations generated by the same model being trained, so the supervision remains closer to the models native reasoning distribution. In contrast, external continuations provide useful signals, but they are less matched to the models own CoT style and therefore offer weaker training signal for learning when to stop. In the RandCut and UniCut ablations, we keep the Detector-selected versus heuristic cutpoints. regeneration process, pair-selection thresholds, and training configuration identical to LoCo, and only change how the cutpoints are selected. Each trace is assigned the same number of cutpoints as in LoCo. Specifically, RandCut selects cutpoints uniformly at random from the trajectory, while UniCut selects them at evenly spaced positions. The shorter continuations are then regenerated and paired following the same procedure as LoCo. This comparison isolates the effect of cutpoint selection and evaluates whether identifying appropriate compression points is important for effective reasoning compression. Both variants can still shorten CoT substantially, but they incur larger accuracy losses because they often compress reasoning at positions where the model still needs additional computation. This effect is especially clear on AIME24 and AIME25, where LoCo preserves the strongest accuracy while matching or exceeding the heuristic variants in overall AUC. These comparisons show that LoCos advantage comes not only from preferring shorter continuations, but from learning that preference at the right reasoning states.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduced LoCo, local preference learning method for reasoning compression that constructs supervision directly at reasoning states where overthinking occurs. Instead of treating compression

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: as global preference over complete trajectories, LoCo freezes the current reasoning prefix, regenerates verified shorter continuations from the same state, and learns state-conditioned continue-orconclude preferences with DPO. Empirically, LoCo shows consistent gains across both mathematical reasoning and code generation. The cross-domain improvements suggest that LoCo primarily reshapes the models preference over reasoning length rather than adding task-specific knowledge. This indicates that effective reasoning compression requires learning when further reasoning is unnecessary at the appropriate reasoning states, rather than simply favoring shorter trajectories.

sections.title: A IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
sections.content: A.1 OVERTHINK DETECTION Source traces. We generate self-sampled reasoning traces from DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B on the math14k training pool, the math-only training set of Zhang et al. (2026b) containing 14,027 questions. We sample three rollouts per question at temperature 0.6 and top-p 0.95, and retain the shortest correct rollout as the source trajectory for each question. Detection, judging, and pair construction all operate on this trajectory, so each question contributes at most one trace. Confidence screening. The complete CoT is fed back to the model as prompt, and we record the top-1 token probability pmax at every position via batched offline vLLM prompt logprobs. Steps are delimited by paragraph breaks. Step confidence ci is the arithmetic mean of pmax over the steps token span, and volatility is vi = (ci ci1)2/4 as in Section 4.2. The four quantiles (q25c, q75c, q25v, q75v) are calibrated once on the models self-generated trace corpus. τ τ Judge re-checking. Every confidence-screened OVERTHINK step is re-checked by Qwen3-30B using vLLM. The judge sees the problem, the preceding steps, the candidate step, and the predicted label, and returns corrected label plus short rationale in JSON. The template is: You are evaluating whether an existing overthink label for one reasoning step is correct. Problem: {question} Previous reasoning steps: {previous_steps} Current reasoning step: {current_step} Predicted label: {predicted_label} Label definitions: - OVERTHINK: this step is wasteful or redundant; removing it would not break the path to the answer.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: - NORMAL: this step is necessary reasoning; removing it would break or weaken the path. - FINAL_ANSWER_WRAPUP: this step mainly wraps up or restates the final answer. Respond in this exact JSON format and nothing else: { "gold_label": "OVERTHINKNORMALFINAL_ANSWER_WRAPUP", "reason": "short reason" } Only judge-confirmed OVERTHINK steps survive. trace with many flagged steps could otherwise dominate regeneration, so each trace keeps at most 10 candidate states, selected by uniform sampling. A.2 EVALUATION DETAIL Evaluation prompts. Each benchmark appends short instruction to the raw problem text, and the result is wrapped by each models native chat template. The five mathematical benchmarks share the instruction Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within boxed{}. The three code benchmarks share the following instruction: Please write solution in Python. ```python code block.

sections.title: Wrap your final code in
sections.content: Following their official protocols, MBPP additionally includes the public tests in the prompt (Your code should pass these tests: tests), while LiveCodeBench appends the provided starter code when applicable. We extract the last Python code block from the complete output, which naturally excludes any code blocks generated within the thinking process, and execute it in sandbox with per-problem timeouts of 10 seconds for MBPP and 6 seconds for LiveCodeBench. CodeContests follows the AlphaCode judging protocol, where outputs are split by whitespace and compared token-wise case-insensitively, with exact matching for integers and tolerance of 105 for floating-point values. A.3 ABLATION CONSTRUCTION This subsection provides the full descriptions of the ablation variants introduced in the main text. All variants use the same question set, pair-selection thresholds, and training recipe as LoCo. Each variant modifies only one construction choice, while differences in pair counts arise naturally from the resulting construction. Global. The Global variant pairs the shortest and longest correct rollouts of the same question. To avoid disadvantaging this variant, its pool is expanded from three source rollouts to eight per question, allowing the selected responses to draw from larger sample of short solutions than the source traces provide. The same savings threshold and top-K selection as LoCo are applied, and the prompt contains only the question, without frozen state. GPT-5.4 Cont. GPT-5.4 continues from the same frozen prefix, provided as an assistant prefill with system instruction to continue the reasoning in the same first-person style without restarting the problem. The continuation is generated directly from the frozen prefix and replaces the selfgenerated chosen continuation only when it is correct and shorter than the rejected continuation. Thus, this variant differs from LoCo only on the chosen side. RandCut and UniCut. Each trace receives the same number of cutpoints as selected by the detector. Cutpoints are sampled from all eligible steps after excluding the first step and the final two

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: steps. RandCut samples uniformly at random. UniCut places the cutpoints on an evenly spaced grid over the trace and snaps each to the nearest eligible step in its segment. Downstream regeneration and pair construction remain unchanged. The detectors cutpoints concentrate late in the trace, with mean relative position of 0.57 and about half occurring in the final 40% of steps. In contrast, RandCut and UniCut cover the trace more uniformly, with mean relative positions of 0.47 and 0.50, respectively. Thus, the heuristic variants tend to compress at earlier, less converged states.
